questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in awarding a grant
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a disappointed grant applicant must show.
questions.stem: Apiary log: The state apiary fund paid twenty-two apiaries for hive relocation and skipped our club's yard; the notice said only that applications were evaluated on programme needs.

options.text: Because the awards are discretionary, the club must show the decision was arbitrary, not a programme judgement
Because the fund is a grant programme, every applicant with a proper hive placement has an automatic right to payment
options.misconception: assumes grant programmes create entitlement

options.text: Because the notice never published criteria, the club is entitled to payment as a matter of due process
options.misconception: treats absent criteria as entitlement

options.text: Because the apiary board has discretion, a reviewing court will substitute its own view of which apiaries deserve help
options.misconception: expects courts to redraw discretionary choices

questions.explanation: A grant programme leaves the agency room to judge, so a challenger must show arbitrariness, not disagreement. The tempting errors are that funding creates entitlement, that missing criteria win relief, or that courts redraw choices.
questions.hint: Ask what makes an agency's choice actionable rather than merely different.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Using block grant money for another purpose
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether block grant funds may be spent on a new purpose.

stimulus.body: A block grant agreement provides a state with funds for 'pollinator habitat improvement' and lists allowable costs including seed, hedgerow planting and maintenance. A separate provision says that funds may be used for other purposes 'consistent with the purposes of this award'. The state now proposes to spend part of the award on public signs announcing the habitat programme.

questions.stem: Colony note: The state wants to spend part of our pollinator block grant on programme signage. Does the award permit that?

options.text: Yes, because the agreement lets funds be used for other purposes consistent with the award's purposes
options.misconception: treats any related purpose as consistent

options.text: No, because the agreement lists allowable costs and signage is not among them
Yes, because the state controls the block grant and may allocate the money as it sees fit
options.misconception: confuses state control with unrestricted use

options.text: No, because block grant money may never be spent on anything the agreement does not name word for word
options.misconception: insists on literal wording and ignores the consistency clause

questions.explanation: A block grant still carries the purposes and cost rules of the award, and the consistency clause does not erase them. The tempting errors are that any related purpose fits, that state control means unrestricted use, or that naming must be literal.
questions.hint: Ask what the award says is allowable and for what purpose.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Prior grants and a new condition
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a new grant condition reaches earlier awards.
questions.stem: Grant file note: A funder wrote asking how a newly announced condition on future pollination contracts could reach the three we signed last year.

answer.exemplar: A new condition binds future awards unless the award document already adopts it, because each grant is a separate arrangement with its own terms. Applying a newly imposed condition to grants already made retroactively raises the question whether the original terms have been altered after the fact. If the funder wants the condition to reach existing contracts, it must either follow the terms those contracts contain or obtain the recipients' agreement to amend them.

questions.explanation: Each award carries its own terms, so a new condition reaches only new money unless it is adopted or the parties agree to amend. The tempting error is that an announced programme condition automatically revises earlier agreements.
questions.hint: Ask which document governs each award.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A data-collection duty aimed at a state
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a federal reporting duty may be imposed on a state.

stimulus.body: A federal agency sent the state apiary board a letter stating: 'All recipients of federal pollination assistance funds, including state agencies, shall file a quarterly hive-movement report with the Department on a form enclosed. This reporting requirement is a condition of federal financial assistance and applies to state recipients as well as private ones.'

questions.stem: Varroa log: The Department wants our state apiary board to file quarterly hive reports as a condition of federal money. What is the issue?

options.text: No issue, because the state is a recipient of federal funds and has accepted the attached condition
options.misconception: treats grant acceptance as consent to any federal demand

options.text: The issue is that a federal agency may impose reporting conditions on state recipients of its own grants
No issue, because the federal government may require reporting from any entity it funds, in any form
options.misconception: assumes funding defeats state sovereignty

options.text: The issue is only that the quarterly form was not published in advance, and the timing alone is unlawful
options.misconception: reduces the problem to advance publication

questions.explanation: A federal agency may write conditions into its own grants, but a reporting demand aimed at a state as such runs into limits the state itself did not agree to. The tempting errors are that funding alone supplies consent, that all demands are permitted, or that only timing is wrong.
questions.hint: Ask whether the duty rests on the grant or on the state itself.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court ordering an agency to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: Determine what remedy a court may give where an agency holds discretion.
questions.stem: Inspection note: Stage one, decide whether the apiary board was required to reopen our relocation grant application; stage two, say what a court could properly order.

options.text: The board had discretion and must be reversed on the merits, and a court should award the grant funds instead
options.misconception: confuses reconsideration with substitution

options.text: The board had discretion, and a court should order the board to pay the grant because the outcome was wrong
options.misconception: asks a court to redo the discretionary call

options.text: The board had discretion, and a court may order it to consider the application on its merits but not to award it
The board was required to reopen the application, and a court should order a new funding round for all clubs
options.misconception: assumes a programme-wide remedy follows one dispute

questions.explanation: Where an agency holds discretion, a court may require the matter to be properly considered but may not make the discretionary call itself. The tempting errors are reversal on the merits, ordering payment, or ordering a programme-wide redo.
questions.hint: Ask whether the court can decide the question or only the process.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Renewal of an expiring rule
questions.learningObjective: Identify the problem with renewing a rule without fresh notice and comment.
questions.stem: Harvest note: The Department's varroa treatment rule was due to expire, and the Department simply extended it by a letter that said nothing about notice or comment.

options.text: The extension is sound, because the rule already exists and renewing it adds no new requirement
options.misconception: treats renewal as free of procedure

options.text: The extension is sound, because the Department may always keep a rule alive while it studies replacements
options.misconception: assumes a study justifies indefinite extension

options.text: The extension is defective unless the Department follows the notice-and-comment route or shows good cause
The extension is void, because every renewal must begin a rulemaking from the very first proposal
options.misconception: requires a fresh start rather than good cause

questions.explanation: A renewal that extends a rule in force normally must repeat the procedure, unless a narrow good-cause exception applies. The tempting errors are that renewal adds nothing, that a study excuses it, or that any defect is total.
questions.hint: Ask what process a continuing rule requires to stay in force.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An agency reading its statute broadly
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a later narrow reading affects an agency's earlier broad construction.
questions.stem: Queen note: I wrote a note for the archive about what happens when an agency later reads its statute more narrowly than it once did.

answer.exemplar: An agency's interpretation binds it for the period in which it was in effect, so a change in construction does not automatically undo actions already taken in good faith under the earlier reading. The later, narrower construction governs going forward and applies to matters still open, and it may be explained by a change in the statute, in the agency's experience, or in the legal landscape. A reviewing court may also reach its own conclusion about the earlier period.

questions.explanation: A later narrow reading governs the future and open matters, but it does not automatically void what was done in good faith under the earlier reading. The tempting error is that a new construction retroactively condemns past conduct.
questions.hint: Ask whether the earlier reading was permissible when it was held.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Guidance that conflicts with a published rule
questions.learningObjective: Resolve a conflict between guidance and a published rule.

stimulus.body: A departmental FAQ published with the hive-registration rule states: 'Where a colony is moved between apiaries within a season, no notice is needed at all, and the destination apiary may record the move on its own paperwork.' The published rule states: 'Any movement of a registered colony must be reported to the Department within ten days.'

questions.stem: Swarm note: Our club moved a colony in June and reported it, but a beekeeper told us the FAQ says no notice is needed. Which text controls?

options.text: The FAQ controls, because a later explanatory document shows how the Department currently reads the rule
options.misconception: lets a FAQ override the published rule

options.text: The published rule controls, and the FAQ cannot excuse the ten-day reporting duty
Neither controls, because the Department should issue a single consolidated text before either can apply
options.misconception: makes a consolidation a condition of application

options.text: The FAQ controls for private apiaries, but the published rule controls for the state programme
options.misconception: invents a split that no document creates

questions.explanation: Guidance explains a rule but cannot subtract from it, so the published ten-day duty stands and the FAQ creates no excuse. The tempting errors are that explanation overrides the text, that consolidation must come first, or that a split applies.
questions.hint: Ask whether the FAQ changes the rule or only describes it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in awarding a grant
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a grant decision becomes arbitrary rather than merely unsuccessful.

stimulus.body: The award notice states: 'Thirty-one apiaries received relocation grants. Applications were ranked on a published scoring sheet; applicants scoring below the cutoff were not funded. The committee noted that two applicants who scored above the cutoff were treated as ineligible because their yards lacked a recorded water source.'

questions.stem: Nectar note: Our scoring sheet put us above the cutoff, but the notice says we were treated as ineligible for lacking a recorded water source. What is the issue?

options.text: Nothing, because eligibility screening always comes before scoring and may be applied afterwards
options.misconception: assumes any screening step is unchallengeable

options.text: The issue is that a stated criterion may not be invented after applications are scored and ranked
Nothing, because the committee may consider any factor it considers relevant to the programme
options.misconception: treats unlimited discretion as lawful

options.text: The issue is only that the cutoff figure itself was never published, and the numbers are the defect
options.misconception: reduces the dispute to a missing number

questions.explanation: Where a scoring scheme is published and relied upon, the agency may not add a new disqualifier afterwards and call the outcome a judgement. The tempting errors are that any screening is unchallengeable, that discretion is unlimited, or that only the numbers matter.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ground for excluding us appeared in the published scheme.

questions.learningObjective: Apply the consistency test to a new use of block grant funds.
questions.stem: Overwinter note: Stage one, decide whether using block grant money for a public education campaign is consistent with the award's purposes; stage two, say what the state must show.

options.text: It is inconsistent, and the state must show the campaign relates to improving pollinator habitat
It is consistent, and the state need only show the campaign was administratively convenient
options.misconception: substitutes convenience for consistency

options.text: It is inconsistent, and the state must show the programme was named in a later award amendment
options.misconception: requires a formal amendment before any use

options.text: It is consistent, and the state must show no other grant could have funded the campaign
options.misconception: invents a least-cost requirement

questions.explanation: The consistency test asks whether the new use serves the purposes of the award, and the state must be able to point to that connection. The tempting errors are that convenience suffices, that an amendment is always needed, or that a least-cost showing is required.
questions.hint: Ask what the state would have to connect the new use to.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Prior grants and a new condition
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a new condition may be imposed on grants already made.

stimulus.body: A funder's notice states: 'Effective immediately, all grantees must use the new hive-movement log attached to this notice, and any award made before today's date is deemed to include this condition.' The signed awards for last season's pollination contracts contain a clause saying: 'Any change to the terms of this agreement requires the written agreement of both parties.'

questions.stem: Package note: The funder says last season's contracts now include its new log condition. What is the answer?

options.text: The condition applies, because the funder states that earlier awards are deemed to include it
options.misconception: treats a unilateral notice as amending an agreement

options.text: The condition does not apply, because the earlier awards require the parties' written agreement to change
The condition applies to future payments only, because the funder controls the money and may stop paying
options.misconception: conflates funding leverage with amendment

options.text: The condition applies, because every funder may set conditions whenever a new programme term is published
options.misconception: assumes publication amends existing contracts

questions.explanation: An award is an arrangement between the parties, and a new term cannot be grafted onto it by unilateral notice where the document reserves changes to writing. The tempting errors are that a notice amends, that funding leverage does the same work, or that publication suffices.
questions.hint: Ask what the signed award says about changing its terms.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A data-collection duty aimed at a state
questions.learningObjective: Separate a condition on federal money from a duty aimed at a state.

stimulus.body: A letter to the state apiary board states: 'The Department requires the Board to compile and transmit an annual inventory of every beehive in the state, including hives kept by private individuals who do not receive federal assistance. The Department explains that this is a general informational collection under the Department's organic statute.'

questions.stem: Pollinator note: The Department demands an inventory of every hive in the state, including ours. What is the problem?

options.text: No problem, because the Department has an organic statute covering bee inspection and inventory work
options.misconception: assumes subject matter alone authorises the duty

options.text: No problem, because inventory work does not burden the state because it does not stop any apiary operating
options.misconception: ignores the burden the duty creates

options.text: The problem is that the duty reaches private hives and the state as such, beyond any grant condition
The problem is only that the Department did not first ask private beekeepers to volunteer their hive counts
options.misconception: reduces the problem to a preference for voluntary data

questions.explanation: A general statutory duty cannot be used to make the state compile a statewide inventory of private property, and a grant condition only governs those who hold the grant. The tempting errors are subject-matter authority, no-operational-burden, and voluntary preference.
questions.hint: Ask who the duty reaches and on what footing.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court ordering an agency to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court may not order an unlawful programme into existence.
questions.stem: Super note: The club asked a court to order the apiary board to fund a hive transport programme that the board's statute does not authorise.

answer.exemplar: A court cannot order an agency to administer a programme its statute does not authorise, because the court cannot confer a power the legislature withheld or direct the expenditure of money the legislature did not appropriate. It may order the agency to act where the agency has discretion and has failed to exercise it lawfully, and it may enforce rights that existing law provides. Where the programme itself is unauthorised, the remedy lies in the legislature, not in the court's order.

questions.explanation: Courts may require lawful action within a grant of power but cannot create the power or the programme. The tempting error is that a court can supply the authorisation the statute withholds.
questions.hint: Ask whether the programme exists in the statute at all.

questions.topic: Renewal of an expiring rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain the good-cause route for extending a rule.

stimulus.body: An order extending an expiring hive-registration rule states: 'The Department finds good cause to extend the rule for ninety days without prior notice and comment because delay would leave an enforcement gap. The Department will accept written comment on this order for thirty days after it is issued.'

questions.stem: Hive box note: The Department extended the registration rule for ninety days without asking for comment first, but says comment will follow. Is that lawful?

options.text: Yes, because a good cause finding permits an interim extension and post-order comment is adequate
No, because an enforcement gap is never good cause for skipping notice and comment
options.misconception: assumes good cause never covers enforcement gaps

options.text: No, because comment after the rule takes effect can never cure a procedural defect
options.misconception: denies post-promulgation comment any value

options.text: Yes, because any interim extension is lawful when the Department could not finish a rulemaking in time
options.misconception: assumes delay alone justifies the shortcut

questions.explanation: A narrow good-cause exception permits a short interim extension, and taking comment afterwards is a recognised part of that route. The tempting errors are that enforcement gaps never qualify, that later comment never cures, or that delay alone suffices.
questions.hint: Ask what the extension is short-lived and reasoned for.

questions.learningObjective: Evaluate a broad agency construction of a statutory phrase.
questions.stem: Requeen note: Stage one, decide whether the apiary board's reading of 'pollinator protection' covers funding municipal tree planting; stage two, say how a court would treat that reading.

options.text: It covers tree planting, and a court will adopt the board's reading if it is reasonable and consistent with the statute
It covers tree planting, and a court must adopt the board's reading because the board administers the programme
options.misconception: treats expertise as conclusive

options.text: It does not cover tree planting, and a court must decide the meaning of the statute for itself
options.misconception: denies any weight to agency construction

options.text: It does not cover tree planting, and a court may only invalidate it without ever construing the statute
options.misconception: assumes invalidation without construction

questions.explanation: A court gives an agency's construction weight when it is reasonable and consistent with the statute, though the court still decides the meaning. The tempting errors are that expertise is conclusive, that the court never construes, or that invalidation comes first.
questions.hint: Ask how much weight a reasonable construction carries.

questions.topic: Guidance that conflicts with a published rule
questions.learningObjective: Decide who must follow the rule when guidance says otherwise.

stimulus.body: An agency bulletin reads: 'Field offices should exercise discretion in enforcing the 30-day hive registration renewal window where an apiary has suffered a swarm loss. questions.stem: Sugar note: A field officer told us to ignore the 30-day renewal window because of swarm losses. What is the effect of that instruction?

options.text: The instruction is valid discretion, so officers may waive the renewal window wherever they judge it appropriate
options.misconception: reads a narrow waiver as general discretion

options.text: The instruction gives officers discretion in a narrow case, but the published window remains the rule elsewhere
The instruction is void in its entirety, so officers have no discretion at all in renewal matters
options.misconception: reads a narrow waiver as no waiver

options.text: The instruction changes the rule, so officers may now apply the waiver wherever they find it reasonable
options.misconception: treats a bulletin as amending a rule

questions.explanation: A bulletin's waiver is limited to the case it describes and cannot rewrite the published window for other cases. The tempting errors are that the waiver generalises, that it vanishes entirely, or that the bulletin amends the rule.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Using block grant money for another purpose
questions.learningObjective: Explain the risk of charging unallowable costs to a grant.
questions.stem: Budget note: I wrote a note for the apiary association about the consequences of spending block grant money on things the award does not allow.

answer.exemplar: A recipient that charges costs the award does not allow risks repayment: the agency may question the cost, disallow it, and reduce the grant by the amount judged unallowable, or decline to make a payment until the matter is resolved. The recipient also loses the ability to argue later that the cost was reasonable, because the award's cost rules govern rather than the recipient's judgement of value. Separating programme money from grant money avoids both problems.

questions.explanation: Unallowable costs can be recovered from the grant and stop future payments, so the award's cost rules govern rather than local judgement. The tempting error is that a reasonable purpose protects an unallowable cost.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost if the expenditure is later disallowed.

questions.topic: An agency reading its statute broadly
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of a later authoritative narrowing of a statute.
questions.stem: Trap note: I wrote a paragraph for the apiary newsletter about what happens when a court narrows a statute the agency had read broadly.

answer.exemplar: A later authoritative narrowing governs the statute from then on, so the agency's broad reading ceases to control, and matters still open must be decided under the narrower meaning. Conduct that was taken in good faith during the period of the broad reading is not automatically invalid, and a reviewing court will examine each such case on its own facts. The practical lesson for recipients is to keep adjusting to the statute as it stands, not to rely on the agency's former reading.

questions.explanation: A later authoritative narrowing governs from then on, and matters still open follow it, though good-faith past conduct is examined case by case. The tempting error is that a narrowing decision voids everything done before it.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to matters that were already decided.

questions.topic: Guidance that conflicts with a published rule

options.misconception: treats published guidance as conclusive

options.text: Yes, because emergency situations justify reading regulation broadly in favour of beekeepers
options.misconception: substitutes equity for the text of the rule

options.text: No, because a guidance sheet cannot expand an exception beyond the words of the regulation
No, because guidance sheets can never mention exceptions to any regulation at all
options.misconception: denies guidance any explanatory function

questions.explanation: Guidance may describe an exception the rule already contains but cannot widen it, and here the sheet reaches further than the regulation's words. questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a condition from a change to the terms of an existing award.
questions.stem: Robbing note: I wrote a note for the association on the difference between adding a condition to a grant and changing the terms of one already made.

answer.exemplar: A condition is a term the grantor attaches to the award and the recipient accepts, so it belongs to the bargain from the start. Changing the terms of an award already made asks the parties to modify an existing arrangement, and the ordinary rules for amendment apply, including any clause in the award requiring written agreement. A funder may also refuse to make a further payment under a term it has validly attached to future money, but that is a different device from amending what was already agreed.

questions.explanation: A condition attaches to an award when it is made, while changing an existing award requires the parties' agreement as the award provides. The tempting error is that a funder's announcement reaches back into agreed terms.
questions.hint: Ask whether the award was made before the condition appeared.

options.misconception: infers continuing force from subject-matter authority

options.misconception: gives agency practice priority over a decision

options.text: Nothing, because only the legislature may change the meaning of a statute it has enacted
options.misconception: denies a court any role in construing statutes

options.text: That the later decision governs from its date while completed earlier actions are not disturbed
That the Department must reopen every completed case because its reading was wrong after all
options.misconception: assumes a later ruling voids settled matters

options.misconception: denies guidance any explanatory role

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in awarding a grant
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a grant applicant's dissatisfaction alone does not establish error.
questions.stem: Extract note: I drafted a short explanation for new members of what a reviewing court will and will not second-guess about grant awards.

answer.exemplar: A reviewing court will not reweigh the competing merits of two apiaries, and it will not substitute its own view of which project deserved money. It will examine whether the process was lawful, whether the criteria were published and applied as written, whether the stated reasons were real, and whether the decision was arbitrary in the sense of capricious or governed by an impermissible consideration. Where those inquiries come out clean, the award stands even if the applicant would have scored differently.

questions.explanation: Courts test process, criteria, reasons and arbitrariness rather than reweighing the merits of competing applicants. The tempting error is that a disappointed applicant's better case is itself a legal wrong.
questions.hint: Ask what the court reviews rather than what it reweighs.

questions.hint: Ask which list the shed would have to appear on.

questions.stem: Bloom note: The Department threatens to withhold funds unless our state produces a certified statewide hive inventory. How should we read this?

options.text: The threat is invalid, because a federal agency cannot condition money on the state's own administrative activity
The threat is valid, because the Department may attach any condition it likes to federal assistance
options.misconception: assumes conditions on money are unlimited

options.text: The threat is valid, because the state chose to accept federal money and therefore owes the inventory
options.misconception: treats acceptance of funds as consent to anything

options.text: The threat is invalid, because federal funds cannot be withheld at all once a state has begun a programme
options.misconception: denies any withholding power

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court ordering an agency to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a court cannot direct the exercise of discretion.
questions.stem: Stand note: I wrote a short note for the association on why a court order cannot tell an agency which way to decide.

answer.exemplar: A court resolves legal questions, including whether the statute permits the action and whether the agency followed its own procedures, but where the statute commits a judgement to the agency, the court cannot make that judgement. An order directing the outcome would take the political and administrative choice away from the body the legislature entrusted with it, and would also deprive the agency of the reasoned explanation its own process requires. The court's role is to require a lawful decision, not to make the choice.

questions.explanation: Courts decide legal questions and require lawful action, while the lawmaker's judgment about which apiary benefits belongs to the agency. The tempting error is that a court with remedial power may simply choose the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask who the statute entrusted the choice to.

It is unsound, because any extension of an expiring rule is automatically a legislative act needing full notice
options.misconception: denies the good-cause exception altogether

options.text: It is unsound, because the Department had to complete the replacement rulemaking before any extension
options.misconception: insists on completed rulemaking first

options.text: It is sound, because good cause exists whenever the alternative would be administrative inconvenience
options.misconception: equates inconvenience with good cause

questions.explanation: A brief, reasoned extension with post-order comment is the recognised interim measure, and the stated purpose here is genuine. The tempting errors are that no exception exists, that replacement must come first, or that inconvenience is good cause.
questions.hint: Ask whether the extension is short, reasoned and open to comment.

answer.exemplar: A condition announced after an award has been made does not alter the terms already agreed, so the recipient is not in breach by following the award as written. A funder may still refuse to make further payments, because it holds the money and may decline to disburse, but that is a decision not to pay rather than a valid amendment of the contract. If the recipient wishes to accept the new condition, the way to do that is to agree an amendment in the form the award requires, so that the record shows the change was accepted.

options.text: No, because only the legislature may change the meaning of a statute it has enacted

options.misconception: treats discretion as including revival

questions.explanation: A successor may construe the statute differently, provided it does not act in defiance of a decision that has already been made. The tempting errors are that practice becomes permanent, that construction is frozen, or that discretion includes revival.
questions.hint: Ask what binds a successor agency most firmly.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Guidance that conflicts with a published rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain why guidance cannot be used to enforce a rule differently.
questions.stem: Bulletin board note: I drafted a paragraph for the apiary newsletter on why guidance cannot be the basis for a citation when it differs from the rule.

answer.exemplar: An enforcement action must rest on a legal requirement the person was actually subject to, and where a published rule and a guidance document say different things, the guidance cannot supply the extra element that the rule omits. Enforcement officers who follow the guidance in a case covered by the rule may find that the notice they issued was not authorised by the source of law it cites. The sound practice is to enforce the rule as published and ask the agency to reconcile its guidance through proper rulemaking or correction.

questions.explanation: Enforcement must rest on the legal requirement in force, and guidance cannot add to or subtract from it. The tempting error is that an officer's reliance on guidance cures a defective notice.
questions.hint: Ask which document supplies the duty that was cited.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in awarding a grant
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether an agency's stated discretion can be reviewed in court.
questions.stem: Ordinance note: The apiary board tells us that grant awards are 'committed to its discretion and not subject to review'.

options.text: The statement is accurate, because a grant programme decision is a matter of judgment and cannot be reviewed at all
options.misconception: denies review of discretionary action

options.text: The statement is accurate, because only the board may assess the needs of the apiary programme
options.misconception: treats expertise as immunity from review

options.text: The statement overstates the position, because arbitrary or unlawful awards remain open to challenge
The statement is inaccurate, because every grant award may be reviewed and the court will substitute its own choice
options.misconception: assumes full merits review of grants

questions.explanation: Discretion is not immunity: an award that is arbitrary or unlawful can still be challenged, even though the merits are not. The tempting errors are that discretion bars review, that expertise does the same, or that courts retry the choice.
questions.hint: Ask whether arbitrariness or unlawfulness leaves review open.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Using block grant money for another purpose
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a new purpose is consistent with a block grant award.
questions.stem: Memo note: Stage one, decide whether using the pollinator block grant to pay for a county-wide flowering hedge is consistent with the award; stage two, say what must be documented.

options.text: It is consistent, and the state need only show the hedge was planted by a qualified contractor
options.misconception: treats contractor qualification as the test for consistency

options.text: It is consistent, and the state need only show the total cost stayed below the remaining balance
options.misconception: treats budget room as the test for consistency

options.text: It is consistent if it serves habitat improvement, and the state must document that connection and the allowable costs
It is inconsistent, because a block grant may be spent only on the purposes literally listed in the award
options.misconception: reads the consistency clause as an exact-match rule

questions.explanation: A new use is permissible when it serves the award's purposes and its costs are allowable, and the state must show both. The tempting errors are that contractor qualification, budget room, or exact wording alone decides the question.
questions.hint: Ask how the new use connects to the award's purposes.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Prior grants and a new condition
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a funder may properly introduce a new condition.

stimulus.body: A funder's notice states: 'Beginning with the 2027 award cycle, successful applicants must hold a current predator-resistant hive certification. Existing recipients are asked to obtain certification by the end of the season as a condition of receiving the final instalment of their current award. The funder confirms that the final instalment has not yet been paid for any current recipient.'

questions.stem: Docket note: The funder says certification is now a condition of our final instalment, which has not been paid. What is the position?

options.text: The condition is properly introduced, because it attaches to a payment the funder has not yet made
The condition is impermissible, because a funder may never impose a condition on money already promised
options.misconception: assumes promised instalments can never be conditioned

options.text: The condition is impermissible, because certification itself is unrelated to the purposes of the pollination award
options.misconception: ignores that a condition may relate to programme quality

options.text: The condition is properly introduced, and it also revises the terms of the rest of our award
options.misconception: assumes a condition reaches back into earlier terms

questions.explanation: A funder may attach a condition to a payment it has not yet made, which is different from rewriting terms already agreed. The tempting errors are that promised money can never be conditioned, that subject-matter relation is irrelevant, or that the condition reaches back.
questions.hint: Ask whether the money has already been paid out.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A data-collection duty aimed at a state
questions.learningObjective: Explain why collecting data from the public is different from collecting it from grantees.

stimulus.body: An agency letter states: 'The Department has revised its information collection to require every beekeeper in the state who sells more than twenty jars of honey annually to report annual yields. The Department notes that collection from private beekeepers is voluntary and that the Department prefers to rely on voluntary submissions wherever possible, while the states are expected to submit complete summaries.'

questions.stem: Bulletin board note: The Department calls collection from beekeepers voluntary but expects states to submit complete summaries. What is the concern?

options.text: No concern, because a request described as voluntary cannot burden anyone and needs no legal basis
options.misconception: takes the label of voluntariness at face value

options.text: The concern is that the state is expected to compile a complete summary without a legal basis for the demand
No concern, because the Department may collect whatever information it finds administratively useful
options.misconception: assumes usefulness supplies legal authority

options.text: The concern is only that the Department should have said the collection was mandatory and explained the penalty
options.misconception: reduces the problem to notice of compulsion

questions.explanation: A demand for a complete state summary needs a legal basis just as much as a demand on beekeepers, and describing the private collection as voluntary does not supply one. The tempting errors are that voluntary requests need no basis, that usefulness suffices, or that only labelling is missing.
questions.hint: Ask what legal basis supports the summary the state must send.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A court ordering an agency to administer a programme
questions.learningObjective: Assess a claim that an agency was required to fund an activity.
questions.stem: Order note: We asked the apiary board to fund hive transport for the county fair, and the board said it had no authority to do so.

options.text: The board is right, because no court may order an agency to do what its statute does not authorise
The board is wrong, because a court may order any agency to carry out any programme a citizen wants
options.misconception: grants courts a general power to direct programmes

options.text: The board is right, because courts may not order discretionary spending at all, even where spending is authorised
options.misconception: denies any remedy for unlawful delay

options.text: The board is wrong, because the club's constitutional right to petition obliges the board to accommodate the request
options.misconception: confuses petitioning with entitlement to funds

questions.explanation: A court cannot require an agency to run a programme the statute does not authorise, though remedies may exist where spending is authorised but wrongly withheld. The tempting errors are a general power over programmes, no remedy for delay, or entitlement from the petition right.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statute authorises the programme at all.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Renewal of an expiring rule
questions.learningObjective: Explain the procedural options available for a rule nearing expiry.

stimulus.body: An internal agency plan states: 'The quarantine rule expires in sixty days. Option one is to begin a rulemaking now with a proposed replacement published in thirty days, allowing the rule to lapse in the interim. Option two is to seek a good-cause extension for up to ninety days, publish an order explaining the extension, accept comment after the order, and complete the replacement rulemaking during that period.'

questions.stem: Register note: The Department has two plans for the quarantine rule. Which plan fits the law?

options.text: Both plans are lawful, because the agency may choose whichever route suits its schedule best
options.misconception: treats both procedural routes as open at will

options.text: Only the lapse-and-replace plan is lawful, because any extension of an expiring rule is unlawful
options.misconception: denies the good-cause route entirely

options.text: Both plans are lawful, provided the extension rests on stated good cause and comment is invited
Neither plan is lawful, because the rule must be amended before it expires rather than replaced
options.misconception: assumes amendment is the only route

questions.explanation: The agency may let a rule lapse and replace it by rulemaking, or use a good-cause extension with a stated reason and an opportunity to comment. The tempting errors are that either route is open at will, that no extension exists, or that amendment is required.
questions.hint: Ask what each option requires the agency to do and publish.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: An agency reading its statute broadly
questions.learningObjective: Decide how a broad construction is judged against the statutory words.
questions.stem: Notice note: The Department reads 'sale of honey' to include honey given away at the village market, and the club says the reading cannot be right.

options.text: The club is right, because a statute is always interpreted against the agency that administers it
options.misconception: inverts the presumption on ambiguous language

options.text: The club is right, because any reading that extends a tax-like term is void without more
options.misconception: invents a general rule against broad readings

options.text: The reading stands if it is reasonable and consistent with the statute, and the court decides the meaning
The reading must be struck down unless the Department can show it was long and consistently followed
options.misconception: makes consistent practice a requirement of validity

questions.explanation: A reasonable, consistent construction is entitled to weight, and the court decides the meaning in the end. The tempting errors are a presumption against the agency, a rule against broad readings, or a long-practice requirement.
questions.hint: Ask who decides the meaning of the statute.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Guidance that conflicts with a published rule
questions.learningObjective: Decide which document a regulated party should follow.
questions.stem: Ledger note: The Department's published rule requires hive registrations to be filed on a single form, and its guidance sheet says registrants may use two forms provided they are filed together.

options.text: The guidance sheet, because a later departmental document reflects the current administrative view
options.misconception: lets guidance override the rule

options.text: The published rule, because guidance may describe a procedure but cannot authorize a departure from it
Whichever the registrant prefers, since the two documents conflict and leave the choice open
options.misconception: suggests a conflict creates an option

options.text: The published rule, because guidance has no force at all and the sheet should be ignored entirely
options.misconception: denies guidance any descriptive function

questions.explanation: Guidance may describe how a rule works but cannot authorise departing from it, so the published single-form requirement stands. The tempting errors are that recency controls, that a conflict creates a choice, or that guidance has no descriptive force.
questions.hint: Ask whether the sheet changes the requirement or only describes it.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Discretion in awarding a grant
questions.learningObjective: Apply the arbitrariness test to a grant decision with an unstated reason.
questions.stem: Petition note: Stage one, decide whether the board's denial of our grant is challengeable; stage two, say what the club must show.

options.text: It is challengeable only if the club shows the decision was arbitrary and the stated reasons were not the real ones
It is challengeable whenever the club can show its application was as good as the winner's
options.misconception: asks the court to compare the merits

options.text: It is not challengeable, because the board gave reasons and discretion covers the rest
options.misconception: treats any stated reason as conclusive

options.text: It is challengeable only if the board ignored the published criteria entirely
options.misconception: narrows the challenge to one kind of error

questions.explanation: A challenge must show arbitrariness, such as a reason that cannot be the real one, rather than merely a better application. The tempting errors are that comparison of merits suffices, that any reason is conclusive, or that only criteria error counts.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a discretionary decision unlawful rather than merely different.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Using block grant money for another purpose
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a recipient should respond to a questioned cost.
questions.stem: Depositary note: I wrote a note for the association about what happens when an agency questions a cost charged to a block grant.

answer.exemplar: The recipient should provide the documentation the award requires, such as the invoice and the explanation of which award purpose the cost served, and it should answer the question in the manner the award prescribes. If the cost was in fact unallowable, the practical remedy is to replace it with an allowable cost and to adjust the accounting for the period, which is usually better than waiting for a dispute to be resolved. A recipient that ignores a query risks disallowance and withheld payments without ever testing its position.

questions.explanation: Documenting the cost promptly is the sound response, and correcting an unallowable charge is often faster than disputing it. The tempting error is that ignoring the query is harmless while the award continues.
questions.hint: Ask what a timely response requires and what delay risks.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: A data-collection duty aimed at a state
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a federal survey demand on a state is permissible.

stimulus.body: An agency survey document states: 'The Department requests that the state apiary board compile and transmit the results of a voluntary statewide hive census, including the names and addresses of individual beekeepers. The Department states that the survey will not be repeated and that participation is not required, while noting that the Department intends to use the results in its report to the legislature.'

questions.stem: Survey note: The Department wants names and addresses of individual beekeepers from our state. What is the issue?

options.text: No issue, because the survey is described as voluntary and the Department will publish only aggregate results
options.misconception: takes the label of voluntariness at face value

options.text: No issue, because the Department may request information from any state for a legislative report
options.misconception: assumes a reporting purpose authorises any demand

options.text: The state may not be compelled to compile a census of private beekeepers for the Department
No issue, because the Department could always obtain the same information by surveying the private beekeepers itself
options.misconception: assumes an agency cannot ask a state at all

questions.explanation: A state cannot be made to compile a census of private individuals for a federal agency, and describing the request as voluntary does not create authority. The tempting errors are that voluntariness answers it, that the reporting purpose authorises it, or that self-collection proves it lawful.
questions.hint: Ask who would have to do the compiling and why.

questions.subject: US_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Prior grants and a new condition
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether a new condition may operate on an award already made.
questions.stem: Interpretive note: The funder's new notice says the new hive standard applies to 'all current and future recipients', and our award was made last autumn.

options.text: The condition applies, because the notice says so and the funder can set terms for its own money
options.misconception: treats the funder's notice as amending the award

options.text: The condition applies, because current recipients are still receiving money under the programme
options.misconception: assumes ongoing payment reaches agreed terms

options.text: The condition does not apply to our award, because the award was made before the condition was announced
The condition applies only if the funder stops paying, because withholding payment revises the award
options.misconception: treats a payment decision as an amendment

questions.explanation: A condition announced after an award was made does not reach back into it, however much money remains to be paid. The tempting errors are that the funder's wording is enough, that continuing payment revises terms, or that withholding payment revises them.
questions.hint: Ask when the award was made and what it said.
